claim: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are currently the highest performing image recognition computer algorithms.
source: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are currently the highest performing image recognition computer algorithms.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the introduction without specific data from this study, representing general knowledge in the field.

claim: The overall design of CNNs reflects the hierarchical structure of the ventral ('form-processing') visual stream.
source: While their overall design reflects the hierarchical structure of the ventral ('form-processing') visual stream (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; LeCun et al., 2015), the visual selectivity (i.e., tuning) of single units within the network are not constrained to match neurobiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; LeCun et al., 2015).

claim: First-layer units in CNNs, following training, often show selectivity for orientation and spatial frequency like neurons in primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Nevertheless, first-layer units in these CNNs, following training, often show selectivity for orientation and spatial frequency (Figure 1; see also Krizhevsky et al., 2012) like neurons in primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 showing Conv1 kernels, citation to Krizhevsky et al., 2012, and established knowledge about V1 neurons.

claim: Selectivity in CNNs becomes increasingly complex and categorical in deeper layers, similar to the progression along the ventral stream.
source: Attempts to visualize features encoded by single units deeper in such networks (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013; Mahendran and Vedaldi, 2014) show that selectivity becomes increasingly complex and categorical, similar to the progression along the ventral stream.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to visualization studies (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013; Mahendran and Vedaldi, 2014).

claim: Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015 found a corresponding hierarchy of visual features between BOLD signals in the human ventral stream and layers within a CNN.
source: Solidifying this idea, Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015 found a corresponding hierarchy of visual features between BOLD signals in the human ventral stream and layers within a CNN.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015.

claim: Artificial networks that perform better at image classification have population-level representations closer to those in area IT.
source: This is not unreasonable given that artificial networks that perform better at image classification also have population-level representations closer to those in area IT (Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Kriegeskorte, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Kriegeskorte, 2015.

claim: V4 is a primary input to IT.
source: V4 is a primary input to IT (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991), yet there has been no systematic examination of whether specific form-selective properties found in V4 emerge within a CNN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Felleman and Van Essen, 1991.

claim: Many V4 neurons are selective for boundary curvature, ranging from concave to sharply convex, at particular angular positions around the center of an object.
source: In particular, many V4 neurons are selective for boundary curvature, ranging from concave to sharply convex, at particular angular positions around the center of an object.
evidence: This is established knowledge about V4 neurons from prior studies, as indicated by the context and citations in the surrounding text (Pasupathy and Connor, 1999; Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; Cadieu et al., 2007).

claim: Many units in AlexNet exhibit translation-invariant boundary curvature selectivity approaching that of exemplar neurons in the primate mid-level visual area V4.
source: Taking the approach of an electrophysiologist to characterizing single CNN units, we found many units exhibit translation-invariant boundary curvature selectivity approaching that of exemplar neurons in the primate mid-level visual area V4.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data and analyses presented throughout the Results section.

claim: For some V4-like units, particularly in middle layers, the natural images that drove them best were qualitatively consistent with selectivity for object boundaries.
source: For some V4-like units, particularly in middle layers, the natural images that drove them best were qualitatively consistent with selectivity for object boundaries.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's visualization analyses, as detailed in the Results section on visualization.

claim: The results identify a novel image-computable model for V4 boundary curvature selectivity.
source: Our results identify a novel image-computable model for V4 boundary curvature selectivity and suggest that such a representation may begin to emerge within an artificial network trained for image categorization, even though boundary information was not provided during training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, representing an inference about the implications of the results.

claim: Boundary curvature representation may begin to emerge within an artificial network trained for image categorization, even though boundary information was not provided during training.
source: Our results identify a novel image-computable model for V4 boundary curvature selectivity and suggest that such a representation may begin to emerge within an artificial network trained for image categorization, even though boundary information was not provided during training.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings that APC-like tuning emerged in AlexNet despite not being explicitly trained for boundary detection.

claim: AlexNet contains over 1.5 million units organized in eight major layers.
source: AlexNet contains over 1.5 million units organized in eight major layers (Figure 2), but its convolutional architecture means that the vast majority of those units are spatially offset copies of each other.
evidence: This is a factual description of the AlexNet architecture, supported by Figure 2.

claim: In the first convolutional layer, Conv1, there are only 96 distinct kernels.
source: For example, in the first convolutional layer, Conv1, there are only 96 distinct kernels (Figure 1), but they are repeated everywhere on a 55 × 55 grid (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a factual description of the Conv1 layer architecture, supported by Figures 1 and 2.

claim: 22,096 unique units were analyzed in the study.
source: These units, plus all units in the subsequent fully-connected layers comprise the 22,096 unique units (Figure 2D) that we analyzed.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the scope of the analysis, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Across the convolutional layers and their sublayers, shape stimuli typically evoked a range of responses that was on average similar to, or larger than, the range driven by ImageNet images.
source: Across the convolutional layers and their sublayers, we found that our shape stimuli typically evoked a range of responses that was on average similar to, or larger than, the range driven by ImageNet images (e.g., Figure 4, Conv1, compare red to dark blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of response distributions, supported by Figure 4.

claim: In the fully-connected layers, natural images drove a larger range of responses than did shapes.
source: In contrast, in the subsequent fully-connected layers, the natural images drove a larger range of responses (Figure 4, FC6, dark blue) than did shapes (red line), and from FC6 onwards the range of responses to shapes was about 1/2 to 1/3 of that for images.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of response distributions, supported by Figure 4.

claim: The wider dynamic range for images in later layers may reflect the sensitivity of deeper units to category-relevant conjunctions of image statistics that are absent in simple shape stimuli.
source: The wider dynamic range for images in later layers may reflect the sensitivity of deeper units to category-relevant conjunctions of image statistics that are absent in our simple shape stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data pattern.

claim: 13% of units across all layers had zero responses to all shape stimuli.
source: Across all layers, 13% of units had zero responses to all shape stimuli and 7% had non-zero response to only one stimulus, that is one shape at one rotation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis of response sparseness.

claim: 7% of units had non-zero response to only one stimulus.
source: Across all layers, 13% of units had zero responses to all shape stimuli and 7% had non-zero response to only one stimulus, that is one shape at one rotation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis of response sparseness.

claim: The responses of many units in the CNN were fit well by the APC model.
source: We found that the responses of many units in the CNN were fit well by the APC model.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the APC model fitting analysis presented in the Results.

claim: FC7-3591 had an APC fit with r-value of 0.77.
source: A second example unit, FC7-3591 (Figure 5C) with a high APC r-value (0.77) had fit parameters (see legend) reflecting selectivity for concavities roughly toward the top of the shape, consistent with most of its preferred shapes (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the APC model fitting analysis, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: There is a clear but modest trend for the cumulative distribution functions of APC r-values to shift rightward for higher layers.
source: For each layer of the CNN, we computed the distributions of the APC fit r-values across units (Figure 5G). There is a clear but modest trend for the cumulative distribution functions to shift rightward for higher layers (orange lines, Figure 5G), indicating that deeper layer units fit better on average to the APC model.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of APC fit distributions across layers, supported by Figure 5G.

claim: The median r-values for layers Conv2 to FC8 were somewhat higher than that for V4.
source: Compared to V4 neurons studied with the same shape set (red line, Figure 5G), the median r-values (corresponding to 0.5 on the vertical axis) for layers Conv2 to FC8 were somewhat higher than that for V4, but the V4 and CNN curves matched closely at the upper range, with the best V4 unit having a higher APC r-value than any CNN unit.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between CNN and V4 data, supported by Figure 5G.

claim: The best V4 unit had a higher APC r-value than any CNN unit.
source: Compared to V4 neurons studied with the same shape set (red line, Figure 5G), the median r-values (corresponding to 0.5 on the vertical axis) for layers Conv2 to FC8 were somewhat higher than that for V4, but the V4 and CNN curves matched closely at the upper range, with the best V4 unit having a higher APC r-value than any CNN unit.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between CNN and V4 data, supported by Figure 5G.

claim: The distribution of noise-corrected V4 r-values has a higher median than that for any of the CNN layers.
source: The distribution of the corrected estimates of the r-values across the V4 population (pink line, Figure 5G) has a higher median than that for any of the CNN layers.
evidence: This is a finding from the noise-correction analysis, supported by Figure 5G.

claim: Training is important for achieving an APC r-value distribution consistent with V4.
source: This suggests that training is important for achieving an APC r-value distribution consistent with V4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between trained and untrained networks.

claim: The APC model largely reflects specific patterns of responses of the units to the shapes, and not an ability of the model to fit any random or noisy set of responses.
source: Thus, the APC model largely reflects specific patterns of responses of the units to the shapes, and not an ability of the model to fit any random or noisy set of responses (see also Pasupathy and Connor, 2001).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the shuffling control analysis, with support from citation to Pasupathy and Connor, 2001.

claim: Conv2-113 has a low translation invariance (TI = 0.7).
source: The largely uncorrelated selectivity at two points within the RF indicates low translation invariance. Thus, despite its high APC r-value (Figure 5A), its low translation invariance diminishes it as a good model for V4 boundary contour tuning. This behavior was typical in layer Conv2, as demonstrated by the position-correlation function averaged across all units in the layer (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from the translation invariance analysis, supported by Figure 6E.

claim: For deeper layers, RFs tend to widen and translation invariance increases.
source: For deeper layers, RFs tend to widen and translation invariance increases.
evidence: This is a general finding from the translation invariance analysis across layers.

claim: Only the deepest four layers (Conv5 to FC8) had median TI values that approximated or exceeded that of the V4 population.
source: For comparison, the cumulative distribution of our TI metric for 39 V4 neurons from the study of El-Shamayleh and Pasupathy (2016) is plotted (red). Only the deepest four layers (Conv5 to FC8) had median TI values that approximated or exceeded that of our V4 population.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between CNN and V4 data, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: The degradation of TI in an untrained network was even more dramatic than the degradation of APC tuning.
source: Furthermore, we computed TI for the same units and stimuli but in the untrained network. We found that the degradation of TI in an untrained network (Figure 7B) was even more dramatic than the degradation of APC tuning (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between trained and untrained networks, supported by Figures 7B and 5H.

claim: It was very rare for any FC-layer unit in the untrained network to exceed the median TI values for those layers in the trained network.
source: Specifically, it was very rare for any FC-layer unit in the untrained network to exceed the median TI values for those layers in the trained network.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison between trained and untrained networks.

claim: The modest rightward shift in the corrected V4 TI distribution relative to the original raw distribution does not change the conclusion that only the deepest several layers in AlexNet have average TI values that match or exceed that of V4.
source: The modest rightward shift in the corrected distribution relative to the original raw distribution (red line) does not change our conclusion that only the deepest several layers in AlexNet have average TI values that match or exceed that of V4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the noise-corrected V4 TI analysis.

claim: There was a high correlation (r = 0.79) between TI measured for horizontal shifts and TI measured for vertical shifts.
source: Our TI metric above was measured for horizontal stimulus shifts; however, we also measured TI for vertical shifts and verified that there was a high correlation between these two (r = 0.79) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), particularly for high TI values.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis comparing TI across different shift directions, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Visualizing the ten most APC-like units in Conv2 revealed selectivity for orientation, conjunctions thereof, or other textures.
source: Visualizing the ten most APC-like units in Conv2 revealed selectivity for orientation, conjunctions thereof, or other textures.
evidence: This is a qualitative finding from the visualization analysis of Conv2 units.

claim: From Conv3 to Conv5, the visualizations of the most APC-like units were more often consistent with an encoding of portions of object boundaries.
source: From Conv3 to Conv5, the visualizations of the most APC-like units were more often consistent with an encoding of portions of object boundaries.
evidence: This is a qualitative finding from the visualization analysis of Conv3-5 units.

claim: In the FC layers, the most excitatory images were revealing about unit preferences, but the deconvolved features provided less insight because power in the back projection was typically widely distributed across the input image.
source: In the FC layers, the most excitatory images were revealing about unit preferences, but the deconvolved features provided less insight because power in the back projection was typically widely distributed across the input image.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the visualization analysis of FC layer units.

claim: Many of the top ten APC-like units in the FC layers fell into two categories: those preferring images with rounded borders facing approximately upwards ('balls' group) and those associated with a concavity between sharp convexities, also facing approximately upwards ('wolf-ears' group).
source: Broadly, many of the top ten APC-like units in the FC layers fell into two categories: those preferring images with rounded borders facing approximately upwards (we refer to these as the 'balls' group) and those associated with a concavity between sharp convexities, also facing approximately upwards (the 'wolf-ears' group).
evidence: This is a qualitative finding from the visualization analysis of FC layer units.

claim: In FC8, the top ten APC units were evenly split between the wolf-ears group and the balls group.
source: In FC8, where there is a one-to-one mapping from units onto the 1000 trained categories, the top ten APC units were evenly split between the wolf-ears group (categories: kit fox, gray fox, impala, red wolf and red fox) and the balls group (categories: ping-pong balls, golf balls, bathing caps, car mirrors and rugby balls).
evidence: This is a finding from the visualization analysis of FC8 units.

claim: The best image drove responses on average about 2 times higher than did the best shape for Conv2-4.
source: Figure 13 shows for the top-10 APC-like units in each layer, that the best image drove responses on average about 2 times higher than did the best shape for Conv2-4, about 4–5 times higher for FC6-7 and more than 8 times higher for FC8.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison of responses to natural images vs. shapes, supported by Figure 13.

claim: The best image drove responses on average about 4–5 times higher than did the best shape for FC6-7.
source: Figure 13 shows for the top-10 APC-like units in each layer, that the best image drove responses on average about 2 times higher than did the best shape for Conv2-4, about 4–5 times higher for FC6-7 and more than 8 times higher for FC8.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison of responses to natural images vs. shapes, supported by Figure 13.

claim: The best image drove responses on average more than 8 times higher than did the best shape for FC8.
source: Figure 13 shows for the top-10 APC-like units in each layer, that the best image drove responses on average about 2 times higher than did the best shape for Conv2-4, about 4–5 times higher for FC6-7 and more than 8 times higher for FC8.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison of responses to natural images vs. shapes, supported by Figure 13.

claim: Only two APC-like units responded better to a shape than to any natural image, but both were Conv4 units selective for bright circular regions.
source: Nevertheless, the selectivity for simple shapes at the final layer appears to be qualitatively consistent with the category label. Notably, only two APC-like units responded better to a shape than to any natural image, but both were Conv4 units selective for bright circular regions (not shown), and the best stimulus was our large circle (Figure 3A, second from upper left).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of responses to natural images vs. shapes.

claim: Just over half (56/109) of V4 neurons were better fit by the APC model than by CNN units.
source: Figure 14 shows the cross-validated, best fit r-values for the APC model plotted against those for the CNN units. Neither model is clearly better on average: just over half (56/109) of neurons were better fit by the APC model, while just under half (53/109) were better fit by a CNN unit.
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-validated comparison between APC model and CNN fits to V4 data, supported by Figure 14.

claim: Just under half (53/109) of V4 neurons were better fit by a CNN unit than by the APC model.
source: Figure 14 shows the cross-validated, best fit r-values for the APC model plotted against those for the CNN units. Neither model is clearly better on average: just over half (56/109) of neurons were better fit by the APC model, while just under half (53/109) were better fit by a CNN unit.
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-validated comparison between APC model and CNN fits to V4 data, supported by Figure 14.

claim: Only 21 of 109 V4 neurons had significant deviations from the line of equality in APC vs. CNN fit quality.
source: Only 21 of 109 neurons had significant deviations from the line of equality (Figure 14, red) and these were evenly split: 11 better fit by the APC model and 10 by the CNN.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of APC model and CNN fits to V4 data, supported by Figure 14.

claim: For 94/109 V4 neurons, the APC model explained more variance than the variance uniquely explained by the CNN.
source: For 94/109 neurons, the APC model explained more variance than the variance uniquely explained by the CNN.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of variance explained by CNN vs. APC model.

claim: The APC model and the CNN explain similar features of V4 responses for most neurons.
source: Overall, we conclude that the APC model and the CNN explain similar features of V4 responses for most neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of APC model and CNN fits to V4 data.

claim: Many units in AlexNet would be indistinguishable from good examples of boundary-curvature-tuned V4 neurons.
source: Making direct comparisons between CNN units and V4 neurons using V4 data from two previous studies (Pasupathy and Connor, 2001; El-Shamayleh and Pasupathy, 2016), we found that many units in AlexNet would be indistinguishable from good examples of boundary-curvature-tuned V4 neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, based on the quantitative comparisons of APC tuning and translation invariance.

claim: APC-like units within middle layers of trained CNNs currently provide the best image-computable models for V4 boundary curvature selectivity.
source: Based on our quantitative criteria and on the qualitative visualization of preferred features identified in natural images, we believe that APC-like units within middle layers of trained CNNs currently provide the best image-computable models for V4 boundary curvature selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined quantitative and qualitative analyses in the study.

claim: Image statistics related to object boundaries may generalize across a wide variety of inputs and may support a broad variety of tasks.
source: Our results suggest that image statistics related to object boundaries may generalize across a wide variety of inputs and may support a broad variety of tasks, thereby explaining the emergence of similar selectivity in such disparate systems.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings regarding why similar selectivity emerges in CNNs and V4.

claim: Training dramatically increased the number of units with V4-like translation invariance, particularly in the FC layers.
source: Training dramatically increased the number of units with V4-like translation invariance, particularly in the FC layers (Figure 7A vs. Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison between trained and untrained networks, supported by Figure 7.

claim: High TI for actual single unit responses is only achieved in tandem with the correct weights.
source: Thus, while CNN architecture is often associated with translation invariance (Fukushima, 1980; Rumelhart et al., 1986; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Serre et al., 2005; Cadieu et al., 2007; Goodfellow et al., 2009; Lenc and Vedaldi, 2014), we find that high TI for actual single unit responses is only achieved in tandem with the correct weights.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison between trained and untrained networks, with support from citations to prior work on CNN architecture and translation invariance.

claim: Translation invariance at the single-unit level is not a trivial result of gross CNN architecture, yet it is crucial for modeling V4 form selectivity.
source: Overall, translation invariance at the single-unit level is not a trivial result of gross CNN architecture, yet it is crucial for modeling V4 form selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses of translation invariance in trained vs. untrained networks.

claim: This work is the first to quantitatively compare the single-unit representation in a CNN to that in a mid-level visual cortical area.
source: Our work is the first to quantitatively compare the single-unit representation in a CNN to that in a mid-level visual cortical area.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's approach, based on comparison to prior work.

claim: Some V4 neurons were better fit directly to a CNN unit than to any APC model.
source: Nevertheless, some V4 neurons were better fit directly to a CNN unit than to any APC model, suggesting there may be V4 representations beyond APC tuning that can be synergistically studied with CNNs.
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-validated comparison between APC model and CNN fits to V4 data.

claim: Finding matches between neuronal selectivity in the brain and artificial networks trained on vast amounts of natural data provides one method for electrophysiologists to validate their findings.
source: Second, finding matches between neuronal selectivity in the brain and artificial networks trained on vast amounts of natural data provides one method for electrophysiologists to validate their findings.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the value of the artiphysiology approach.

claim: The findings support the hypothesis that an encoding of boundary curvature in single units may be generally important for the representation of objects.
source: For example, our findings support the hypothesis that an encoding of boundary curvature in single units may be generally important for the representation of objects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that APC-like tuning emerged in AlexNet.
